content: The proportion of infants living with HIV who might be incorrectly classified as having an indeterminate status is estimated to be between 8% and 13%. Meanwhile, the proportion of HIV-uninfected infants who might unnecessarily begin treatment is estimated to be between 2% and 7%. The cycle threshold (Ct) values, which are used in nucleic acid-based assays, vary depending on the specific assay and cannot be directly transferred between different technologies or assays. Infants who are true positives but have low levels of viraemia generally experience slower disease progression. These infants should be monitored closely until a definitive diagnosis is made. The Guideline Development Group has determined that it is more acceptable to have a higher proportion of true-positive infants misclassified as indeterminate rather than having false-positive results. This is because all indeterminate test results should be followed up with repeat testing as soon as possible before initiating lifelong treatment. Introducing an indeterminate range in diagnostic testing will enhance the accuracy of nucleic acid-based early infant diagnosis. This approach is expected to reduce the number of HIV-negative infants who might otherwise start unnecessary lifelong treatment, as most false-positive results will fall within the indeterminate range rather than being classified as positive. This strategy will also help minimize confusion and challenges in interpreting subsequent discordant test results, especially if the infant was initially classified as positive and had already started treatment. By reducing false-positive results, the indeterminate range will decrease unnecessary treatment and encourage confirmatory testing for all non-negative results. It will also prompt corrective actions to address potential contamination during sample collection or laboratory processing. However, potential harms include the need for additional specimens, which could delay treatment initiation and increase the risk of losing HIV-positive infants to follow-up care if their initial test results are indeterminate. Nevertheless, infants with low levels of viraemia, who represent a small proportion of HIV-positive cases within the indeterminate range, are expected to progress more slowly to morbidity and mortality. Implementing an indeterminate range may also reduce healthcare workers' confidence in early infant diagnosis programs if high rates of resampling and retesting are required. However, cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that introducing an indeterminate range is more effective than the current standard of care, as it requires minimal additional resources for retesting non-negative specimens compared to the cost of unnecessary lifelong treatment. The use of an indeterminate range is expected to improve equity by ensuring that HIV-negative infants are not subjected to unnecessary lifelong treatment. It will also facilitate access to appropriate treatment for infants correctly identified as HIV-positive. Surveys of healthcare workers, program managers, and people living with HIV indicate that the indeterminate range is highly acceptable, provided that the meaning of indeterminate results is clearly explained to mothers and caregivers. Clear guidance on the need for resampling and retesting is essential to avoid confusion. Feasibility studies suggest that implementing an indeterminate range is practical, especially if repeat testing can be performed on the same specimen. Most indeterminate results are expected to be resolved with repeat testing of the same sample, reducing the need for new specimens and associated delays. If the same specimen cannot be retested, a new sample should be collected and tested promptly. For point-of-care technologies where direct application of the sample to the cartridge is required, a new sample should be taken and tested immediately to confirm positive results. This recommendation to use an indeterminate range for more accurate infant diagnosis should be applied to all nucleic acid-based tests for infants under 18 months of age, including testing at birth and six weeks of age. Recent evidence suggests reconsidering the use of HIV serology assays to rule out infection in asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants at nine months of age. Changes in transmission dynamics, policies, and practices have complicated the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for determining infection status. Enhanced postnatal prophylaxis and maternal treatment policies have led to reduced viral loads and delayed antibody development in HIV-infected infants. Additionally, maternal infection during late pregnancy or the postnatal period may result in insufficient passive transfer of HIV antibodies to the infant. These concerns are supported by findings from Uganda and Kenya, where 15–40% of children under two years of age identified as HIV-infected had positive nucleic acid tests (NAT) but negative RDT results. In this context, a WHO expert group convened in May 2018 emphasized the importance of testing mothers to accurately assess infant exposure status. They advocated for nucleic acid-based testing instead of serology at nine months for all symptomatic and asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants to determine HIV status before 18 months of age. Early infant diagnostic assays typically measure the presence of the virus using real-time nucleic acid-based technologies, which report cycle thresholds (Ct). The Ct value, representing the PCR cycle at which amplification is observed, is inversely correlated with the viral load in the sample. However, Ct values vary by assay and cannot be directly compared across different technologies. Additional considerations may be needed for countries using plasma samples instead of whole blood or dried blood spots, as the latter sample types often capture intracellular nucleic acids, potentially increasing detected viral levels. Research priorities include gathering more evidence on the impact of implementing an indeterminate range in populations with increased drug exposure and enhanced infant prophylaxis, earlier testing near birth, different sample types, variations in prevalence, and different viral subtypes. Further research is also needed on effective communication strategies for healthcare workers, mothers, and caregivers, as well as optimal standard operating procedures for managing indeterminate test results. The WHO plans to disseminate these guidelines through printed and web-based formats, supported by peer-reviewed publications of the systematic reviews underlying the recommendations. A policy brief will accompany the guidelines, and WHO will incorporate them into the next update of the consolidated ARV guidelines. Key dissemination steps include presenting the recommendations at international conferences, holding workshops for country adaptation, and developing tools to assist countries in setting priorities. The uptake of these recommendations in national guidelines will be assessed in 2020.
